name: Protein-heavy growth diet

lead: Adolescents in height communities eat plenty of protein and calories, often from meat, dairy and eggs, so that nutrition does not limit growth and they reach their full genetic height. Unlike many height ideas, it relates to a documented determinant of growth: childhood nutrition.

Growth depends on adequate energy and amino acids alongside genetics and hormones. Chronic childhood malnutrition is documented to delay growth and reduce adult height, national average height correlates with protein quality, and Guatemalan Maya children raised in the US were about 10 cm taller than peers in Guatemala, attributed largely to better nutrition and health care. Studies of extra protein in already well-nourished teens were not found.

paras: People build meals around protein foods such as meat, dairy, eggs and fish, eat enough total calories, and pair it with sleep and training during the growth years. Results are measured over the full course of puberty rather than weeks.
A balanced diet is ordinary; people with kidney or metabolic conditions follow medical guidance on protein. Extreme diets carry their own nutritional risks.

chain: Adequate protein and calories in puberty
angle.text: Eating enough protein and calories through puberty supplies what growth needs, helping you reach your full genetic height. Childhood nutrition is a documented determinant of growth; whether protein beyond normal needs adds more has not been tested.

lead: A protein-heavy growth diet is an approach discussed in height communities in which adolescents eat adequate or high amounts of protein and calories, often from meat, dairy and eggs, so that nutrition does not limit growth and they reach their full genetic height. Unlike many height claims, it relates to a documented determinant of growth: childhood nutrition.

Reference sources describe adult height as 60 to 80 percent heritable and state that chronic malnutrition in childhood and adolescence can delay growth and reduce adult height. National average height is described as correlating with protein quality, with countries eating more meat, dairy, eggs and fish tending to be taller. A study of Guatemalan Maya children found those raised in the United States about 10 cm taller than peers in Guatemala, attributed largely to better nutrition and health care.

Children need more protein than adults because it supports growth and development [1]. Sources do not report that eating more protein than needed in an already well-nourished adolescent increases height beyond genetic potential.
infobox: About 0.8 g/kg body weight; children need more [1]

paras: Proponents encourage sufficient calories and protein-rich foods during puberty so nutrition is not a limiting factor. Some also discuss calcium and vitamin D. Protein comes from animal sources such as meat, dairy, eggs and fish and from plant sources such as legumes, nuts and whole grains [1].

Childhood and adolescence are described as critical periods in which undernutrition can reduce adult height even without a medical condition. Population comparisons link taller average stature with diets richer in animal protein, though differences between populations may reflect genetics, lifestyle or both. Growth is described as ending on average around age 15 or 16 in females and 18 to 19 in males. Severe protein-energy malnutrition is linked with failure to grow and with kwashiorkor [1].

Health authorities have not set a tolerable upper limit for protein. Surplus amino acids are broken down in the liver and excreted as urea, excess protein may raise urinary calcium and possibly kidney stone risk, and people with chronic kidney disease are advised to limit protein [1].

No studies found testing a protein-heavy diet specifically as a height-maximising protocol in well-nourished adolescents. Population and malnutrition research, summarised in reference works, links poor childhood nutrition with reduced adult height.

lore.intro: In height forums, adequate nutrition is often described as a lever for teenagers, in contrast with supplements or devices.

claims.claim: Eating enough protein and calories lets you reach your full genetic height.
Extra protein beyond normal needs adds height.
